questions.question: Let $f\colon D\to\mathbb{R}$ be convex on a convex set $D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ and let $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}$. Which statement about the level set $\{\boldsymbol{x}\in D\colon f(\boldsymbol{x})=\alpha\}$ is correct?
options: It is convex, being a subset of the convex sublevel set $L_{\alpha}=\{f\leq\alpha\}$.
It is convex, being the intersection of the sets $\{f\leq\alpha\}$ and $\{f\geq\alpha\}$.
It need not be convex, even though the sublevel set $L_{\alpha}=\{f\leq\alpha\}$ always is.
It need not be convex when $L_{\alpha}$ is unbounded, but it is convex when $L_{\alpha}$ is bounded.

questions.question: For convex $f$ on a convex set $D$, the proof that $L_{\alpha}=\{f\leq\alpha\}$ is convex takes $\boldsymbol{p},\boldsymbol{q}\in L_{\alpha}$, $\lambda\in[0,1]$ and uses $f(\lambda\boldsymbol{p}+(1-\lambda)\boldsymbol{q})\leq\lambda f(\boldsymbol{p})+(1-\lambda)f(\boldsymbol{q})$. What justifies the next step $\lambda f(\boldsymbol{p})+(1-\lambda)f(\boldsymbol{q})\leq\alpha$?
options: The bounds $f(\boldsymbol{p})\leq\alpha$ and $f(\boldsymbol{q})\leq\alpha$ with weights $\lambda,1-\lambda\geq0$ summing to $1$.
The convexity of $D$, which places the point $\lambda\boldsymbol{p}+(1-\lambda)\boldsymbol{q}$ inside the domain $D$.
The convexity of $f$, applied a second time to the two values $f(\boldsymbol{p})$ and $f(\boldsymbol{q})$.
The equalities $f(\boldsymbol{p})=f(\boldsymbol{q})=\alpha$, as both points lie on the edge of the set $L_{\alpha}$.

questions.question: A convex function $f$ on a convex set $D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ and a level $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}$ define the strict sublevel set $S=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in D\colon f(\boldsymbol{x})<\alpha\}$. Is $S$ convex, and why?
options: It is convex only if $f$ is strictly convex, which makes the convexity inequality strict.
It need not be convex, as it is not closed and only the closed set $L_{\alpha}$ is guaranteed convex.
It need not be convex, as removing the level set $\{f=\alpha\}$ from $L_{\alpha}$ can break convexity.
It is always convex: the proof for $L_{\alpha}$ goes through with a strict inequality in the last step.

questions.question: A convex function $f\colon\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}$ satisfies $f(\boldsymbol{x})\geq2$ for every $\boldsymbol{x}$. What does the result that sublevel sets of convex functions are convex give for $L_1=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n\colon f(\boldsymbol{x})\leq1\}$?
options: Nothing, because the result only covers levels $\alpha$ that $f$ actually attains as a value.
$L_1=\varnothing$, which is convex by convention, so the result holds without exception.
$L_1=\mathbb{R}^n$, because the condition $f(\boldsymbol{x})\geq2>1$ holds at every point.
$L_1=\varnothing$, which is not convex, because it contains no segment between two points.

questions.question: The result that sublevel sets $L_{\alpha}=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in D\colon f(\boldsymbol{x})\leq\alpha\}$ of a convex function $f$ are convex is stated for a convex domain $D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$. What is the role of the convexity of $D$ in its proof?
options: It makes $f$ continuous on all of $D$, so that $L_{\alpha}$ is a closed set.
It makes $L_{\alpha}$ nonempty for every level $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}$.
It puts $\lambda\boldsymbol{p}+(1-\lambda)\boldsymbol{q}$ in $D$, so that $f$ is defined there.
It makes $L_{\alpha}$ convex directly, as a subset of the convex set $D$.

questions.question: Which subset of $\mathbb{R}^2$ is guaranteed to be convex because it is a sublevel set of a convex function?
For the convex function $f(x)=x^2-4x$ on $\mathbb{R}$, which set is the sublevel set $L_5=\{x\in\mathbb{R}\colon f(x)\leq5\}$?

The closed halfspace $H=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon 2x_1-x_2\geq3\}$ is to be written as a sublevel set $\{\boldsymbol{x}\colon f(\boldsymbol{x})\leq\alpha\}$ of an affine function $f$. Which choice of $f$ and $\alpha$ is correct?

For the convex function $f(\boldsymbol{x})=(x_1-1)^2+2(x_2+1)^2+3$ on $\mathbb{R}^2$, which description of the sublevel sets $L_{\alpha}=\{\boldsymbol{x}\colon f(\boldsymbol{x})\leq\alpha\}$ is correct?
options: $\varnothing$ for $\alpha\leq3$, and a filled ellipse for $\alpha>3$
$\{(1,-1)\}$ for $\alpha\leq3$, and a filled ellipse for $\alpha>3$
$\varnothing$ for $\alpha<3$, $\{(1,-1)\}$ for $\alpha=3$, a filled ellipse for $\alpha>3$
$\varnothing$ for $\alpha<3$, $\{(1,-1)\}$ for $\alpha=3$, an ellipse curve for $\alpha>3$

questions.question: For the concave function $g(\boldsymbol{x})=4-|x_1|-|x_2|$ on $\mathbb{R}^2$, which set is the superlevel set $U_2=\{\boldsymbol{x}\colon g(\boldsymbol{x})\geq2\}$?

Let $g_1,\dots,g_m$ be convex functions on $\mathbb{R}^n$ and $\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_m\in\mathbb{R}$. Which argument correctly shows that $C=\{\boldsymbol{x}\colon g_i(\boldsymbol{x})\leq\alpha_i,\ i=1,\dots,m\}$ is convex?
options: $C$ is the sublevel set of the convex sum $g_1+\dots+g_m$ at the level $\alpha_1+\dots+\alpha_m$.
$C$ is the intersection of the convex sublevel sets $\{g_i\leq\alpha_i\}$, and intersections keep convexity.
$C$ is the sublevel set of the convex function $\max_i g_i$ at the level $\max_i\alpha_i$.
$C$ is closed, since each $g_i$ is continuous on $\mathbb{R}^n$, and closed subsets of $\mathbb{R}^n$ are convex.

questions.question: Let $f$ and $g$ be convex functions on $\mathbb{R}$ and $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}$. Which set is guaranteed to be convex for all such $f$, $g$ and $\alpha$?
Let $f\colon\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}$ be convex and $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}$. Why is the sublevel set $L_{\alpha}=\{\boldsymbol{x}\colon f(\boldsymbol{x})\leq\alpha\}$ closed?
options: Because $L_{\alpha}$ is convex, and every convex subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is closed.
Because $L_{\alpha}$ is bounded, and bounded convex subsets of $\mathbb{R}^n$ are closed.
Because the weights $\lambda,1-\lambda$ keep the inequality $f\leq\alpha$ along every segment.
Because $f$ is continuous on $\mathbb{R}^n$ and $L_{\alpha}$ is the preimage of $(-\infty,\alpha]$.

questions.question: The function $f(x)=\frac{1}{x}$ is convex on its domain $D=(0,\infty)$. Which points of $D$ satisfy $f(x)\leq2$, that is, what is the sublevel set $L_2$?
For the convex functions $f(x)=x^2-2x$ and $g(x)=|x-3|$ on $\mathbb{R}$, which set is $C=\{x\in\mathbb{R}\colon f(x)\leq3,\ g(x)\leq1\}$?

The function $h(\boldsymbol{x})=x_1^2-x_2^2$ on $\mathbb{R}^2$ is not convex, so the result on sublevel sets does not apply to $L_1=\{\boldsymbol{x}\colon h(\boldsymbol{x})\leq1\}$. Which pair of points lies in $L_1$ while their midpoint does not?

Let $f\colon\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}$ be convex, $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}$, $L_{\alpha}=\{\boldsymbol{x}\colon f(\boldsymbol{x})\leq\alpha\}$ and $S_{\alpha}=\{\boldsymbol{x}\colon f(\boldsymbol{x})<\alpha\}$. Which statement holds for every such $f$ and $\alpha$?

Let $f$ be convex on a convex set $D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$, with epigraph $\operatorname{Epi}(f)$, hypograph $\operatorname{Hypo}(f)$ and the projection $\pi(\boldsymbol{x},t)=\boldsymbol{x}$ from $\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}$ to $\mathbb{R}^n$. Which set equals $L_{\alpha}=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in D\colon f(\boldsymbol{x})\leq\alpha\}$ for every such $f$ and every $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}$?
On $D=[0,2]$ let $f(x)=x$ for $0\leq x<2$ and $f(2)=5$; this $f$ is convex on $D$. For which levels $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}$ is the sublevel set $L_{\alpha}=\{x\in D\colon f(x)\leq\alpha\}$ not closed?

A student claims: if every sublevel set $L_{\alpha}=\{x\in\mathbb{R}\colon f(x)\leq\alpha\}$ of a function $f\colon\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ is convex, then $f$ is convex. Which function is a counterexample to this claim?
